findings.title: SQL injection in new repo helpers — parametrised queries planned, but tech-spec must reaffirm contract for ALL new SQL
findings.description: All proposed new repo helpers (`list_recent_pending_fingerprints`, `list_recent_published_fingerprints`, `update_published_fingerprint`, `is_pair_rate_limited`, `mark_pair_pinged`, `is_dedup_degraded_rate_limited`, `mark_dedup_degraded_pinged`) operate on operator-trusted columns (link, source_name, model_fingerprint). Code-research §14.H shows the proposed SQL is fully parametrised: `conn.execute("... WHERE fetched_at >= datetime('now', ? || ' days')", (f"-{int(days)}",))` casts days to int before formatting, and link values go through `?` placeholders. The `bot_state` k/v scheme uses compound keys like `softflag_pair:{new_link}\n{existing_link}` — these are inserted as VALUES via `?` (matches `outage_state.py` pattern). Nothing in tech-spec proposes string-concatenated SQL. RISK is minor and forward-looking only: the implementer needs to follow code-research §14.H verbatim. If the implementer slips and uses f-string SQL for the `days` argument or any link, injection becomes possible. RECOMMENDATION: keep code-research §14.H signatures as the binding reference; reviewer must verify all four helpers + the migration block use `?` placeholders or `int()` casts on numeric args. No string-formatted SQL anywhere.
findings.location: Section: Decisions 5,6 / Data Models / Implementation Tasks 2,4 (pending_articles_repo.py changes)
findings.impact: If implementer accidentally uses f-string for the `days` arg or the link parameter, a malicious link in `published_articles` (extremely improbable — links come from trusted RSS) could escape into the WHERE clause. Bounded by the fact that link content cannot reach DDL paths.
findings.recommendation: Adopt the exact signatures from code-research §14.H. Every numeric arg passed as `f"-{int(days)}"`. Every link, fingerprint JSON, ISO-8601 timestamp passed as `?` placeholder. Add a code-review checklist item: 'no f-string SQL added in this PR'. The migration block ALTERs are static literals (Decision 11, code-research §14.G) — safe.

findings.title: ReDoS-safe bounded quantifiers — verify final compiled regex matches code-research §14.B exactly
findings.description: Decision 3 commits to bounded quantifiers and the final hardened pattern is in code-research §14.B.3: `(?:(?:19|20)\d{2}\s{1,3})?(?P<brand>aston\s{1,2}martin|...|amc|bmw)(?:[\s\-]{1,3}(?P<model>[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9\-]{1,24}))?`. All quantifiers are explicitly bounded: `\d{2}` (year), `\s{1,3}` (separator), `\s{1,2}` (multi-word brand), `{1,24}` (model token). No nested `+` over groups, no `*` anywhere in the model-extractor regex. The alternation is left-to-right linear, the brand list is finite (~35 entries), and Python's `re` engine is backtracking but with bounded quantifiers it stays linear in input length. The 1ms-on-5KB-body performance budget claim (code-research §14.J.2) is consistent with no catastrophic backtracking. RISK: the tech-spec body (Decision 3 line 104) shows a slightly different shape than code-research §14.B.3 — Decision 3 mentions `{0,24}` and `{0,2}` for repeated model words after the first. Code-research §14.B.4 says one-token-after-brand is the chosen rule (no `{0,2}` extra-word capture). The two phrasings need to be reconciled in the implementation; the implementer must pick code-research §14.B.3 as the canonical pattern. ADDITIONAL CHECK: brand strings inside the alternation are HARDCODED in source (not user input), so the alternation itself cannot be injected.
findings.impact: If implementer adds an unbounded `+` or nested unbounded `*` (e.g. `(\w+)+`) when translating Decision 3 prose into code, a crafted 10KB body could trigger catastrophic backtracking — but the AC9 degraded-mode wrapper catches ANY exception, including a Python `RecursionError` or a stalled regex, so the worst case is a slow cron tick (10s+ stall) before the article passes through. Operator pings via E016. No DoS amplification because cron is sequential.
findings.recommendation: Implementer must use code-research §14.B.3 verbatim as the compiled regex. Add a unit test `test_redos_safety` that runs the regex against a 10KB pathological input (`'a' * 10000 + 'Toyota Camry'`) and asserts wall-clock <100ms. Already implicit in the Testing Strategy line 'Long body bounded performance (regex completes <10ms on 10KB body)' — make sure that test fails closed (asserts elapsed time, not just completion).

findings.title: Backfill SSRF surface bounded by domain-substring dispatch in fetch_full_article
findings.description: `backfill_fingerprints.py` calls `news_bot.fetch_full_article(entry_stub)` where `entry_stub = {'link': row['link'], 'source_name': row['source_name'], 'title': ..., 'published': ''}` (code-research §14.E.3 lines 998-1019). The `link` is read from `published_articles.link` — operator-trusted (came through accepted RSS feeds, passed multiple gates, was published to channel). `fetch_full_article` dispatches via `urlparse(link).netloc` substring match (`news_bot.py:1448-1481`): `'autoevolution.com' in domain`, `'blogspot.com' in domain`, etc. PRE-EXISTING SSRF surface (not introduced by this tech-spec): a malicious link like `https://blogspot.com.attacker.example/path` has netloc `blogspot.com.attacker.example` which CONTAINS the substring `blogspot.com` and would dispatch to `t_hunted_source.fetch_t_hunted_article`. Same for `autoevolution.com.attacker.example`. But: such a link could ONLY end up in `published_articles` if an attacker controlled the RSS feed, which is a pre-existing trust assumption (RSS feed URLs are operator-configured in `load_feeds()`). This tech-spec does NOT add new ingestion paths. The backfill only re-walks rows already in the DB. RISK: if an attacker ever compromises an RSS feed and plants a malicious link, the backfill script (operator-run) becomes a delayed re-trigger of the same SSRF — but the same SSRF already runs on every cron tick that re-fetches the article anyway. RECOMMENDATION (defense in depth): tech-spec could add a `urlparse(link).netloc.endswith(('autoevolution.com', 'blogspot.com', 'lamleygroup.com', 'corporate.mattel.com', 'orangetrackdiecast.com'))` allowlist in `fetch_full_article` — but this is OUT OF SCOPE for cross-source-dedup. Flag for a separate hardening ticket.
findings.impact: Pre-existing risk. The backfill does not widen the SSRF surface — it walks links that already passed through `fetch_full_article` once when they were published. Worst case: a poisoned `published_articles` row triggers an outbound request to an attacker-controlled host during backfill, but no secrets are sent (curl_cffi uses chrome user-agent, no auth headers).
findings.recommendation: (1) For THIS feature: no change required — the entry_stub shape (code-research §14.E.3) reads only DB columns, no user-supplied values inject. Verify implementer uses `row.get(...)` for stub fields, not dict literal expansion that could leak unexpected keys into the fetcher. (2) DEFENSE IN DEPTH (separate ticket): tighten `news_bot.fetch_full_article` domain match from `in domain` to `netloc == 'www.autoevolution.com' or netloc.endswith('.autoevolution.com')` style allowlist. Not blocking this feature.

findings.title: Admin-ping templates E014/E015/E016 — plain text parse_mode=None confirms no Markdown/HTML injection vector
findings.description: Tech-spec Decision 7 specifies three new alert builders. They emit text rendered through `send_admin_notification` (news_bot.py:377-412). VERIFIED: `send_admin_notification` calls `bot.send_message(..., text=safe_message)` with NO `parse_mode` kwarg (line 403-406), and the comment at line 396-402 explicitly documents that Markdown was rejected 2026-04-30 BECAUSE of the spoofing risk where article-derived text could rewrite the visible message via crafted `[label](url)` syntax. So: even though E014 templates embed `{new_link}`, `{existing_link}`, and `{models}` from article-derived content (which is operator-trusted but could theoretically contain Telegram-Markdown control chars), Telegram renders them as plain text. No injection. CHECK: `_redact_text` is applied to the message before send (line 388), redacting bot tokens / API key shapes — so even if a model name in an article happened to look like a Telegram bot token (`123456:ABC-DEF...` shape), it would be `***`-redacted. The `[INSTANCE_LABEL]` prefix uses operator-controlled config, not article content. RISK: very low. RECOMMENDATION: confirm in test_admin_alerts that the new builders don't accidentally introduce HTML/Markdown formatting attempts (no `<b>`, no `*bold*`) — Decision 7 says columnar Russian text mirroring E006 which is plain text. The E006 builder pattern (admin_alerts.py:95-107 per code-research §3.3) is the safe reference. Reviewer should diff new builders against E006 shape.
findings.impact: None directly — plain text rendering blocks Markdown injection. Belt-and-suspenders via _redact_text catches accidental token leakage.
findings.recommendation: Mirror E006 builder shape exactly (per code-research §3.3-3.4). No `parse_mode='Markdown'` or `'HTML'` anywhere in new code paths. The test_admin_alerts tests should assert the builder returns a `str` that contains the link verbatim with no escape transformation (confirms the link is being trusted as plain text).

findings.title: Token redaction — verify no new logging path emits `model_fingerprint` JSON to a stream that bypasses _TokenRedactingFilter
findings.description: Project-wide pattern: `_TokenRedactingFilter` is attached to root logger + named noisy loggers (news_bot.py:339-350). Any new `logger.info(...)` / `logger.exception(...)` introduced by this tech-spec inherits the filter automatically. New logging sites: (a) `_check_cross_source_dedup` block + degraded-mode `logger.exception(...)` (tech-spec line 47), (b) backfill stdout summary (tech-spec lines 65-76), (c) E016 ping content. CHECK: `bot_state` keys contain article LINKS only (`softflag_pair:{new_link}\n{existing_link}`, `dedup_degraded_last_pinged_at`). Article links are not secrets per project convention (operator confirmed in memory note: 'bot_state keys contain links (URLs are not secret)'). Fingerprint JSON contains brand/model tokens — also not secrets. The `model_fingerprint` JSON `_dumps()` uses `ensure_ascii=False` — matches existing convention, no encoding pitfall. RISK: very low. SCENARIO TO WATCH: if a malformed `published_articles` row contains an accidental token-shaped substring in the title (e.g. a real Telegram bot token leaked into the title — extremely improbable, would require an upstream RSS feed to publish a token), the `_TokenRedactingFilter` catches it before any handler writes. `backfill_fingerprints.py` uses `logging.basicConfig(...)` (code-research §14.E.2 line 961-962) — IMPORTANT: this attaches a StreamHandler to the root logger, which inherits the filter installed at module load. As long as `backfill_fingerprints.py` does `import news_bot` (which it must for `fetch_full_article`), the filter is installed via news_bot module-load side effect (line 339-356). VERIFY in implementation that the import order is `import news_bot` BEFORE `logging.basicConfig(...)`, so the filter is attached to the root logger when the basicConfig handler is created.
findings.impact: Theoretical: if backfill_fingerprints.py is run with `python3 backfill_fingerprints.py` and somehow logs before `news_bot` imports (e.g. argparse-level logging at module top), tokens in error messages could escape redaction. Operationally unlikely.
findings.recommendation: In `backfill_fingerprints.py`, place `import news_bot` (or `from news_bot import fetch_full_article`) BEFORE the `logging.basicConfig(...)` call inside `main()`. Alternatively, explicitly attach `news_bot._TOKEN_FILTER` to the root logger after basicConfig (defensive). Add a unit test asserting that an error logged from backfill_fingerprints when given a token-shaped error message gets `***`-redacted in caplog output.

findings.title: Concurrent cron tick + operator-run backfill — race window on update_published_fingerprint not addressed by lockfile
findings.description: Concern raised in the briefing: 'What if cron tick and operator-run backfill race?' Tech-spec Risks table line 330 acknowledges this and says: 'ALTER on SQLite is atomic-ish; backfill is operator-initiated AFTER the first cron tick completes init_schema migration. Operationally separated.' This addresses ALTER-vs-runtime, but NOT the steady-state race where: backfill is running its slow per-row loop (50 rows × ~3s/fetch + 1s sleep = ~3 min), and during that window a cron tick fires, processes a NEW article from autoevolution, and `insert_pending` writes a row with a fresh fingerprint. SQLite serialises writes via implicit transaction locking — no corruption. BUT: backfill's read-then-write pattern (`SELECT WHERE model_fingerprint IS NULL ...` then `UPDATE ... WHERE link=?`) is NOT atomic. If a cron tick simultaneously runs the dedup gate (read `list_recent_published_fingerprints`), the new row may or may not have a fingerprint depending on transaction ordering. This is NOT a security issue — worst case is one missed dedup comparison on one article during the 3-min backfill window. ANALYSIS: AC11 says backfill is operator-run on PROD ONCE after first deploy. Operator runs it ONCE (~5 min total). The chance of a cron tick landing inside that window AND fetching an article AND that article being a cross-source dupe of a backfilled-this-second row is vanishingly small. Operationally acceptable. RISK: minor design gap, not security-critical. RECOMMENDATION (optional hardening): add a `bot_state` key `backfill_in_progress=<iso>` set at script start and cleared at end (similar pattern to outage_state). The cron job's dedup gate could read this and defer/skip dedup for the tick. OR — simpler — accept the race per Risks line 330 and document it. The user-spec Risk 2 'False negative (дубль проскочит)' is already mitigated by 'manual archive review 1× / month'.
findings.impact: One dedup comparison may miss a freshly-backfilled fingerprint during the ~3-min backfill window. One false-negative dupe possible on first-deploy day. No data corruption, no integrity breach, no SQL race.
findings.recommendation: (Optional) Add a `bot_state` key `dedup_backfill_in_progress` set at backfill start and cleared in a `finally` block. Cron tick's dedup gate reads it and if set, falls through (degraded mode — passes article unchanged, but does NOT trigger E016). This adds ~10 LoC and one helper. Decision rationale: operator-run-once vs cron-runs-every-tick — operationally simple to just run backfill at a quiet hour. Document in operator-runbook: 'run backfill_fingerprints.py during a low-traffic window, ideally right after a fresh cron tick has completed.'

findings.title: Backfill resource budget reasonable — operator-controlled, no DoS surface
findings.description: Briefing concern: 'Resource exhaustion: backfill loops 50 articles with fetch_full_article (5KB+ HTML each), 1s sleep — no DoS surface here, but operator runs it.' CONFIRMED: backfill is operator-initiated, not triggered by user input. Loop walks `published_articles WHERE model_fingerprint IS NULL AND published_at >= datetime('now', '-14 days')`, bounded to ~50 rows (code-research §14.E.3 line 986). Each `fetch_full_article` is ~3s fetch + 1s sleep. Total budget: ~50 × 4s = ~3 min. NO DoS amplification: (a) cron is sequential — backfill running does not double cron concurrency. (b) memory: per-article HTML ~5KB × 50 = 250KB peak — trivial. (c) network: 50 requests with 1s polite sleep — well under Cloudflare's per-IP rate limit. (d) DB: ~50 single-row UPDATEs — SQLite handles this in <1s of pure DB time. RISK if `--days` accepts unbounded values: an operator typo `--days 14000` would scan all of `published_articles` (potentially 5000+ rows after years of operation), making ~15000s = 4hrs of fetches. Hits Cloudflare rate-limit at scale, partially fails, but no security impact. RECOMMENDATION: cap `--days` to a reasonable max (e.g. 90) in `_build_parser()` argparse — `type=lambda x: min(int(x), 90)` or `choices=range(1, 91)`. Defensive against operator finger-fumble.
findings.impact: Low. Operator-controlled invocation. Worst case: operator typo causes a long-running fetch loop that gets Cloudflare-throttled. No data loss, no privilege escalation, no SSRF amplification.
findings.recommendation: In `_build_parser()`, validate `--days` with a sanity bound: `def _bounded_days(s): n = int(s); assert 1 <= n <= 90; return n` and `type=_bounded_days`. Catches typos. Also clamp the SELECT to `LIMIT 500` defensively. Add a unit test `test_backfill_days_bounded`.
